problem: Let $k$ and $d$ be positive integers. Prove that there exists a positive integer $N$ such that for every odd integer $n\gt N$, the digits in the base-$2n$ representation of $n^k$ are all greater than $d$.

grading_scheme.desc: Uses the base-2n representation of $n^k$ to find a closed form expression of each digit $a_i=\left\lfloor \frac{n^k}{(2n)^i}\right\rfloor mod\ (2n)$
grading_scheme.title: Initial closed form expression for each digit

grading_scheme.desc: Transforms the digit expression into a easily boundable one by interchanging the floor and modulo operations.

grading_scheme.desc: Correctly bounds the aforementioned expression, usually by showing the numerator is divisible by n, so that $a_i>=\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2^i}\right\rfloor$\|.$
grading_scheme.title: Bounding the expression

grading_scheme.desc: Chooses a provably sufficiently large $N$. The point is not awarded if it has not proven that n^k has at most k digits.
grading_scheme.title: Finishing

sample_solution:
We claim one such $N$ is $\boxed{N=2^{k-1}(d+1)}$. Begin by letting $a_i$ be the digit at the $i$th position from the right (0-indexed) of $n^k$ in base $2n$; i.e., $a_0$ is the units digit. Obviously, $a_i=0$ for all $i\ge k$, since $n^k\lt (2n)^k$. We WTS $a_i\gt d$ for each $i=0,1,\dots,k-1$, and observe the following:
\[ a_i=\left\lfloor\frac{n^k}{(2n)^i}\right\rfloor\text{ mod }2n=\left\lfloor\frac{n^{k-i}}{2^i}\right\rfloor\text{ mod }2n=\left\lfloor\frac{n^{k-i}\text{ mod }2^{i+1}n}{2^i}\right\rfloor. \]Note that the numerator is a positive multiple of $n$, since 1) $k-i\gt 0\implies n\mid\gcd(n^{k-i},2^{i+1}n)$ and 2)
($n$ is odd) $2^{i+1}n\nmid n^{k-i}$. Thus,
\[ a_i=\left\lfloor\frac{n^{k-i}\text{ mod }2^{i+1}n}{2^i}\right\rfloor\gt d \quad\iff\quad n^{k-i}\text{ mod }2^{i+1}n\ge n\ge2^i(d+1), \]which is true since $n\gt N=2^{k-1}(d+1)$ and $k-1\ge i$. $\square$

We compute
\begin{align*}
\binom{n-1}{i} &= \frac{(n-1)!}{i! (n-i-1)!} \\
&= \frac{(n-1)(n-2)\cdots (n-i)}{i!} \\
&= \prod_{j=1}^i \frac{n-j}{j},
\end{align*}so$$\binom{n-1}{i}^k = \prod_{j=1}^i \left(\frac{n-j}{j}\right)^k.$$If $p_l \nmid j,$ then $p_l \nmid n-j$ as well since $p_l \mid n.$ Thus $j$ has a modular inverse modulo $p_l^{e_k},$ so we can say$$\left(\frac{n-j}{j}\right)^k \equiv \left(\frac{-j}{j}\right)^k \equiv (-1)^k \equiv 1 \pmod{p_l^{e_k}}$$because $k$ is even. We claim that the answer is $\boxed{\text{all even integers}}.$

Proof that odd $k$ fail: Just take $n = 2$ and get $2^k + 2$ is divisible by $3,$ which implies $2^k \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ This can only happen if $k$ is even.

Proof that even $k$ work: Substitute $n-1$ in place for $n$ in the problem; we then must prove that$$\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \binom{n-1}{i}^k$$is an integer for all positive integers $n.$ Call $n$ $k$-good if $n$ satisfies this condition. Letting $\omega(n)$ denote the number of not necessarily distinct prime factors of $n,$ we will prove that all positive integers $n$ are $k$-good by induction on $\omega(n).$ The base case is trivial since if $\omega(n) = 0,$ then $n = 1,$ which vacuously works.

Now suppose that the result was true for all $n$ such that $\omega(n) \le a.$ Let the prime factorization of $n$ be $p_1^{e_1} \cdot p_2^{e_2} \cdots p_m^{e_m},$ where $p_1, \dots, p_m$ are distinct primes and $e_1, \dots, e_m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $e_1 + \dots + e_m = a+1.$ We will show that$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \binom{n-1}{i}^k \equiv 0 \pmod{p_l^{e_l}}$$for all $1 \le l \le m,$ which finishes the inductive step by CRT.

We compute
\begin{align*}
\binom{n-1}{i} &= \frac{(n-1)!}{i! (n-i-1)!} \\
&= \frac{(n-1)(n-2)\cdots (n-i)}{i!} \\
&= \prod_{j=1}^i \frac{n-j}{j},
\end{align*}so$$\binom{n-1}{i}^k = \prod_{j=1}^i \left(\frac{n-j}{j}\right)^k.$$If $p_l \nmid j,$ then $p_l \nmid n-j$ as well since $p_l \mid n.$ Thus $j$ has a modular inverse modulo $p_l^{e_k},$ so we can say$$\left(\frac{n-j}{j}\right)^k \equiv \left(\frac{-j}{j}\right)^k \equiv (-1)^k \equiv 1 \pmod{p_l^{e_k}}$$because $k$ is even. Hence the terms in this product for which $p_l \nmid j$ contribute nothing to the binomial coefficient.

If $p_l \mid j,$ then we have$$\frac{n-j}{j} = \frac{\frac{n}{p_l} - \frac{j}{p_l}}{\frac{j}{p_l}}.$$Reindexing the product in terms of $\frac{j}{p_l},$ we get$$\binom{n-1}{i}^k \equiv \prod_{j'=1}^{\lfloor i/p_l \rfloor} \left(\frac{n/p_l - j'}{j'}\right)^k \equiv \binom{n/p_l}{\lfloor i/p_l \rfloor}^k \pmod{p_l^{e_l}}.$$Therefore, plugging back into our sum gives$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \binom{n-1}{i}^k \equiv p_l \sum_{i=0}^{n/p_l - 1} \binom{n/p_l - 1}{i}^k \pmod{p_l^{e_l}}.$$By the inductive hypothesis, the sum on the right-hand side is divisible by $p_l^{e_l - 1},$ so the entire sum is divisible by $p_l^{e_l}.$ This completes our inductive step.

Recall the identity:

Define the $P$ person's partitions as bubbles. Then we get a matching between the $n$ people $P$ and the first person's $n$ bubbles $B$. Connect a person to a bubble if they value that bubble as more than $1$, so one person is connected to all the bubbles on this bipartite graph $G \subset P \times B$. If Hall's condition is satisfied on these people, take that matching to win. Else, there exists some set $X$ of people such that they match less than $|X|$ bubbles. Remove that set, and repeatedly remove any set with $|N_G(X)| \lt  |X|$. We must end up with some non-empty set of people $M$ such that $M$ and $N_G(M)$ have a matching, and no person in $P \setminus M$ matches any bubble in $N_G(M)$. In this case, we may take a matching on $M$ and $N_G(M)$, and remove this matching and the corresponding bubbles. Since the remaining people aren't connected to these bubbles, this inductively preserves the score condition for them. This is further explained below:


Call the $s$ people who you are about to delete settled. For the people who aren't settled, you need to make sure they lose exactly $s$ groups in the deletion, and that each of their remaining groups still has value at least 1. For each of the $s$ settled people, delete the group they match with one at a time. Call the group we are about to delete $G$. By the hypothesis (this is what the Hall's was for), the $n-s$ unsettled people value $G$ at most $1$. In particular, none of these unsettled people will possess a group that is contained strictly within $G$. They either own two adjacent groups whose border lies inside $G$, or they own one group that contains $G$ (or is equal to $G$).
Suppose an unsettled person falls under the former case. Before, the two adjacent groups had a total value of at least $2$, and after deleting $G$, at most $1$ total value of cupcake was deleted from the union of those groups. Gluing the remains of those two groups together thus creates a new group with total value at least $1$, maintaining the condition. Then, they simply glue the two remains of this group together with another group to the left. Let the $m$ cupcakes be referred to as "bubbles," denoted by the set $\mathcal{B}$. We construct a bipartite graph $G$ between the set of $n$ people, $\mathcal{P}$, and the set of $m$ bubbles, $\mathcal{B}$. An edge exists between a person $p \in \mathcal{P}$ and a bubble $b \in \mathcal{B}$ if and only if $p$ values $b$ at least $1$. Note that the first person connects to all bubbles in $\mathcal{B}$.

If $G$ satisfies Hall's Marriage Condition, a perfect matching exists, providing a complete solution. If not, there exists a subset $X \subseteq \mathcal{P}$ such that $|N_G(X)| \lt  |X|$. We iteratively remove such subsets. Let $M$ be the non-empty set of people remaining after this process. It follows that $M$ satisfies Hall's Condition with respect to its neighborhood $N_G(M)$, allowing for a matching between them. Crucially, no person in $\mathcal{P} \setminus M$ has an edge connecting to any bubble in $N_G(M)$.

We designate the members of $M$ as "settled" (let $s = |M|$) and assign them the bubbles in $N_G(M)$ via the matching. We then remove these $s$ bubbles and the settled people. We must verify that this removal preserves the problem structure for the remaining $n-s$ "unsettled" people. Specifically, we must ensure that after the removal of the $s$ bubbles, the unsettled people can reduce their partition count by exactly $s$ while maintaining intervals of value at least $1$.

Consider the removal of a single bubble $B \in N_G(M)$. By the construction of $M$, any unsettled person $u \in \mathcal{P} \setminus M$ has no edge to $B$, implying $u$ values $B$ at strictly less than $1$ (or at most $1$). Consequently, $u$ cannot have an interval strictly contained within $B$. Two cases arise for the topology of $u$'s intervals relative to $B$:

\begin{enumerate}

\item \textbf{Boundary Intersection:} The boundary between two of $u$'s adjacent intervals lies inside $B$. The sum of the values of these two original intervals was at least $2$. Since the total value of $B$ is at most $1$ for $u$, removing $B$ removes at most $1$ unit of value from the union of these two intervals. Merging the remnants of these two intervals yields a single new interval with value at least $1$. This operation successfully reduces $u$'s interval count by $1$.

\item \textbf{Containment:} One of $u$'s intervals fully contains $B$ (or is equal to $B$). Removing $B$ creates a gap in this interval. We merge the remaining fragments of this interval with an adjacent interval (e.g., the one to the left). The resulting combined interval retains a value of at least $1$.
\end{enumerate}

Repeating this process for all $s$ bubbles in $N_G(M)$ reduces the problem to $n-s$ unsettled people and $n-s$ remaining bubbles. The solution then follows by induction.
